title: Friends, women, books
hook: three kinds of company, and books the most constant (Essays 3.3)

segments.voice: Yesterday, of repentance, and your line was steady change. Did your one small change happen, quietly, without a speech? Day one thousand one hundred sixty-five.

Who do you actually spend your hours with? Not who you'd list on a form. Who's really there, day after day, when you look back over a week? Montaigne asks himself that question in the next essay of book three, and the French title calls it three kinds of commerce, meaning three kinds of dealings, three kinds of company. He names them without fuss: friends, women, and books. Then he does what he always does. He weighs each one honestly: what it gives him, and what it costs.
screen: `WHO'S REALLY THERE?` → `THREE KINDS OF COMPANY.` → `WHAT EACH GIVES AND COSTS.`

segments.voice: First, friends. Montaigne prizes real friendship, the kind where two minds can talk freely and sharpen each other. But he admits it's rare and depends on finding the right person, and on that person staying. A gift of chance. Second, the company of women. Here he writes frankly, as a man of his time, about love and attraction between men and women. It is sweet, he says, and it stirs the body and the feelings, but it is also restless and can unsettle the mind. Readers today notice how his era frames it. What he's weighing, in his own way, is closeness that is lovely and never fully in his control. Third, books. This is the company he says is steadiest. Books are there when he wants them and wait quietly when he doesn't. They don't sulk if he ignores them. They console him in solitude and help him pass dull hours. And he tells us where they live: his library in the tower, where he walks while he thinks, because, he says, his thoughts fall asleep if he makes them sit. Fourth, the catch. Even books have a fault, he says: they exercise the mind and leave the body idle. So no single company is enough. Laid out like that, it's a useful map. A friend who talks back. A closeness that warms you, whatever shape it has in your life. And something steady that's always on the shelf. Each one feeds something the others can't.
screen: `FRIENDS: RARE, A GIFT OF CHANCE.` · `LOVE: SWEET, BUT RESTLESS.` · `BOOKS: THERE WHEN YOU WANT THEM.` · `EVEN BOOKS LEAVE THE BODY IDLE.` · then, large: `THREE COMPANIES.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: spend a moment with each kind of company. Sit, and breathe. First, bring to mind a friend who talks back to you honestly, and let yourself be glad they exist. Then bring to mind someone close, whose warmth you feel, whatever that closeness looks like for you. Then think of a book, or a song, or a page that has stayed with you, always there on the shelf. Three companies. Let each one sit with you for a few breaths. The bell holds the time.
Friends. The first of Montaigne's three companies: rare, a gift of chance, and worth weighing beside the other two. Today's word.
Your line: three companies. Today, give a little time to each: send a friend a message, be present with someone close, and read one page of something. Day one thousand one hundred sixty-five.

howItsDone: Readers of Montaigne's essay on three kinds of company often take it as a quiet inventory: friends, love, and books, each weighed for what it gives and what it costs.
